To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the nomadic Turkana people in Kenya have their own culturally specific conceptions of childhood development and early childhood education, and that the Western models of early childhood education that are currently being implemented in Kenya are not consistent with those conceptions.

The nomadic pastoralists of the Turkana region of Kenya have developed and sustained their culture over millennia through a process of naturalistic learning in which the acquisition of knowledge, skills and values is embedded in the everyday experiences of children as they participate in and observe the activities of their families and communities.
the Turkana nomadic community in northwest Kenya has a well-defined system of early childhood development, which is based on a holistic understanding of child development.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the early childhood education system in Kenya is in need of serious reformation, and that the reformation needs to begin by recognizing the value of local knowledge and practices in early childhood education.

the early childhood development curriculum in Kenya needs to be reconceptualized in order to reflect local cultural conceptions and values, to be grounded in the practical realities of children's everyday lives, and to be responsive to the needs of children's families.

the integration of indigenous knowledge and naturalistic learning processes into early education programs and services can enhance the relevance and effectiveness of those programs and services, as well as their acceptance by local communities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the educational value of children's learning in their home and community contexts is often unrecognized, undervalued, and underutilized by ECE professionals and policymakers.
the early education of young African children can be grounded in local conceptions and practices of child development and learning.
early childhood education in Africa should not only be grounded in local knowledge, but should also be designed to promote the development of children's indigenous cultural knowledge and practices.
